title: Matthew 4:18–22
context: Walking by the Sea of Galilee, Jesus calls Simon Peter and Andrew from their nets, then James and John from their boat with Zebedee; all four leave immediately and follow Him.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Classic comment on walking by the Sea of Galilee, Jesus calls Simon Peter and Andrew from their nets, from both sides of the debate.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Simon called Peter, and Andrew his brother - Why did not Jesus Christ call some of the eminent Scribes or Pharisees to publish his Gospel, and not poor unlearned fishermen, without credit or authority? Because it was the kingdom of heaven they were to preach, and their teaching must come from above: besides, the conversion of sinners, though it be effected instrumentally by the preaching of the Gospel, yet the grand agent in it is the Spirit of God.
arminian.source: Commentary on the New Testament (on Matt 4:18–22)

reformed.quote: As this history is placed by Luke after the two miracles, which we shall afterwards see, an opinion has commonly prevailed, that the miracle, which is here related by him, was performed some time after that they had been called by Christ. But the reason, which they allege, carries little weight: for no fixed and distinct order of dates was observed by the Evangelists in composing their narratives.
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 4:18–22)

verses.text: Walking by the sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers: Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew, his brother, casting a net into the sea; for they were fishermen.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesus walks, sees, and finds brothers at ordinary work—casting nets. Discipleship begins in a workplace, not a seminary lobby.

The call meets people where they are. Grace notices fishermen; response will soon be asked in freedom under that grace.
verses.reformedNotes:
The King is walking and seeing. Simon and Andrew are located by providence at the nets when the word comes.

Vocation becomes the stage for calling. “He saw” is not casual glance; it is the Shepherd identifying those He will summon.

verses.text: He said to them, “Come after me, and I will make you fishers for men.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Come after me” is personal command; “I will make you” is promise. Jesus reshapes their trade into mission—people, not only fish.

Arminians find a serious invitation with enabling: follow, and He will form you. Both affirm: discipleship is Jesus’ making, not self-reinvention.
verses.reformedNotes:
Imperative and future meet: follow, and I will make. The Maker of fishers speaks first; transformation is His work.

Effectual calling is audible here. The same voice that commands also creates the new craft—missionaries formed by the King’s word.
verses.keyContrast: Both affirm Jesus’ initiative and the promise to remake them. Arminians emphasize a sincere, grace-enabled call they freely obey; Calvinists stress an effectual call that infallibly produces followers and fishers.

verses.text: They immediately left their nets and followed him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Immediately—nets left, path taken. Delay would have been another sermon; obedience is the commentary.

James and John leave the boat and their father at once, and that is what responsive faith looks like. Grace that calls also enables leaving; responsibility remains to walk after Him without postponing forever.
verses.reformedNotes:
Immediacy marks the power of the call. Nets that defined them are released in a moment.

When the Shepherd calls, sheep follow. Leaving is evidence of a word that works—not mere advice filed for later.

verses.text: Going on from there, he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother, in the boat with Zebedee their father, mending their nets. He called them.
verses.arminianNotes:
Another pair, same pattern: He sees, He calls. James and John are mending nets with their father—family business interrupted by the King.

The call is personal and costly. Grace does not erase fathers and boats; it reorders loves so Christ comes first.
verses.reformedNotes:
Going on, seeing, calling—Jesus’ initiative repeats. Zebedee is present; the summons still lands on the sons.

The same sovereign voice that took Peter and Andrew now claims James and John. The church’s core is gathered by calling, not by committee.

verses.text: They immediately left the boat and their father, and followed him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Boat and father left immediately. Loyalty to Jesus outranks livelihood and even family claims when they compete.

Arminian readers preach costly, willing discipleship under grace. The leave-taking is choice enabled by the call—shared with Reformed readers that following Jesus may rearrange every tie.
verses.reformedNotes:
Immediate departure from boat and father displays the call’s force. Priority shifts because the King has spoken.

Discipleship can mean leaving good gifts for a greater Lord. The Father who calls also holds families; yet when His Son summons, obedience does not negotiate forever.
verses.keyContrast: Both honor costly, immediate following. Arminians often emphasize grace-enabled free response that leaves nets and father; Reformed readers often emphasize effectual calling that produces such leaving as its fruit.
